Dynamic diagram (deployment view): Private cross-cloud API access from Azure to AWS.
Requirement: Azure integration workloads privately call internal AWS API Gateway REST APIs. DNS resolution and API traffic are distinct flows, labeled A and B.

Azure Cloud contains three spoke VNets, one each for dev, test and prod. Callers are Azure Function Apps or Logic Apps in those spokes. Show a representative Function App with the Logic Apps alternative and all three environments stated; this does not mean three extra application flows. Spokes connect to a hub VNet containing Azure Firewall and Azure VPN Gateway, and to a separate DNS extension VNet containing Azure DNS Private Resolver inbound and outbound endpoints. The outbound endpoint has a DNS forwarding ruleset for *.execute-api.{region}.amazonaws.com targeting the IP addresses of the AWS Route 53 Resolver inbound endpoint.

An IPsec site-to-site VPN joins Azure VPN Gateway to AWS Site-to-Site VPN attached to AWS Transit Gateway. Draw the VPN connection explicitly between the clouds. AWS Cloud and a Region contain a network services account and three workload accounts, one per environment (dev, test, prod). Transit Gateway is an infrastructure node in the network services account, attached to three VPCs: ingress VPC 10.1.0.0/20, inspection VPC 10.2.0.0/24, and egress VPC 10.3.0.0/20. Ingress contains Route 53 Resolver inbound endpoint and the private hosted zone execute-api.{region}.amazonaws.com, associated with the ingress VPC, not attached to the resolver endpoint. Inspection contains AWS Network Firewall performing IDPS. Egress contains an execute-api interface VPC endpoint. Each workload account contains a private API Gateway REST API protected by a resource policy and backed by Lambda; Lambda runtime remains unspecified, so use AWS Lambda as its technology. The VPC endpoint is the private entry to the API Gateway APIs.

Flow A, DNS: the representative Azure caller queries the Private Resolver inbound endpoint. Private Resolver uses its outbound endpoint/ruleset to forward the execute-api query toward the Route 53 inbound endpoint over DNS port 53. The stated traffic path traverses Azure Firewall, Azure VPN Gateway, the IPsec VPN, Transit Gateway and AWS Network Firewall before reaching the ingress resolver. The resolver uses the private hosted zone and returns the execute-api interface endpoint's private IP; fold that response into the query label. Describe traffic-forwarding legs as DNS routing, not software calls initiated by the transit devices. DNS queries also pass AWS Network Firewall in this synthetic fixture. The Transit Gateway/VPC routing details beyond that specified forwarding path are not given; do not invent route tables.

Flow B, API call: the Azure caller sends HTTPS port 443 traffic through Azure Firewall and Azure VPN Gateway, across the IPsec VPN to Transit Gateway, through Network Firewall inspection and toward the execute-api interface endpoint. The endpoint provides access to the private API Gateway in the corresponding workload account, subject to its resource policy; API Gateway invokes Lambda. Route 53 Resolver outbound endpoints do not forward HTTPS requests and no Route 53 outbound endpoint is retained in this fixture. Preserve the distinct roles of DNS and application routing.

Architecture notes/tables: the forwarding rule and its target resolver IPs; environment list dev/test/prod; firewall allowances per environment from spoke subnet to Route 53 inbound endpoint IPs on port 53 and from spoke subnet to *.execute-api.{region}.amazonaws.com on port 443, applying to Azure Firewall and AWS Network Firewall. Region and actual resolver IPs are parameters, not fixed values to invent. Number flow A and B independently and explain their colors and dashed DNS/solid HTTPS notation in a legend. Model VPCs and accounts as deployment nodes and network devices/endpoints as infrastructure nodes.

2.description:
The diagram is titled “Dynamic diagram (deployment view): Private cross-cloud API access from Azure to AWS.” Azure integration workloads privately call internal AWS API Gateway REST APIs. Flow A resolves DNS; flow B carries the corresponding environment’s API request.

The Azure Cloud deployment boundary contains a DNS extension VNet, a hub VNet, and three spoke VNets for dev, test, and prod. The dev spoke VNet is marked representative and contains a representative integration caller, a container using Azure Function Apps. Logic Apps is an alternative caller. The test and prod spoke VNets each state that their integration workload uses Function Apps or Logic Apps and follows the same representative A/B flow. All three spoke VNets connect to the hub VNet and the separate DNS extension VNet. A single depicted caller represents the environment-specific integration workload and selects its corresponding AWS workload account.

The DNS extension VNet contains two infrastructure nodes: a Private Resolver inbound endpoint and a Private Resolver outbound endpoint, both using Azure DNS Private Resolver. Its outbound endpoint has a DNS forwarding ruleset: *.execute-api.{region}.amazonaws.com forwards to {Route 53 inbound endpoint IPs}. DNS uses port 53, and the resolver IPs are parameters. The hub VNet contains an Azure Firewall infrastructure node and an Azure VPN Gateway infrastructure node.

The AWS Cloud deployment boundary contains a Region: {region} deployment boundary. Within that region are one network services account and separate dev, test, and prod workload accounts, all depicted as deployment nodes. The network services account contains an AWS Site-to-Site VPN infrastructure node, an AWS Transit Gateway infrastructure node, and three VPCs: ingress VPC 10.1.0.0/20, inspection VPC 10.2.0.0/24, and egress VPC 10.3.0.0/20. The ingress VPC contains a Route 53 inbound endpoint, using Amazon Route 53 Resolver, and a private hosted zone using Amazon Route 53. The private hosted zone is execute-api.{region}.amazonaws.com and is associated with the ingress VPC. The inspection VPC contains an AWS Network Firewall — IDPS infrastructure node, using AWS Network Firewall. The egress VPC contains an execute-api interface VPC endpoint, using AWS VPC endpoint.

The AWS Transit Gateway has attachments to the ingress, inspection, and egress VPCs. Transit Gateway/VPC routing details beyond the depicted forwarding path are unspecified. Azure VPN Gateway and AWS Site-to-Site VPN are joined by an IPsec site-to-site VPN across the Azure/AWS boundary.

Each of the dev, test, and prod AWS workload accounts contains an “Internal API” software system boundary. Each Internal API boundary contains two containers: that environment’s private REST API, implemented with Amazon API Gateway and marked “Resource policy protected,” and that environment’s API backend, implemented with AWS Lambda. There are three private REST APIs and three Lambda backends in total. Lambda runtime is unspecified.

Flow A is drawn with blue dashed directed arrows for DNS queries and DNS traffic routing on port 53. Its numbered path is:
A1: The representative integration caller sends a query to the Azure Private Resolver inbound endpoint, labeled “query [DNS 53]; reply: private endpoint IP.”
A2: The inbound endpoint sends an execute-api query to the Azure Private Resolver outbound endpoint, labeled “execute-api query [DNS 53].”
A3: The outbound endpoint routes DNS traffic to Azure Firewall, labeled “DNS routing [53].”
A4: Azure Firewall routes DNS traffic to Azure VPN Gateway, labeled “DNS routing [53].”
A5: Azure VPN Gateway routes DNS traffic across the cloud boundary to AWS Site-to-Site VPN, labeled “DNS routing [53 / IPsec VPN].”
A6: AWS Site-to-Site VPN routes DNS traffic to Transit Gateway, labeled “DNS routing [53].”
A7: Transit Gateway routes DNS traffic to AWS Network Firewall — IDPS, labeled “DNS routing [53 / IDPS].”
A8: AWS Network Firewall routes DNS traffic to the Route 53 inbound endpoint in the ingress VPC, labeled “DNS routing [53].”
A9: The Route 53 inbound endpoint resolves against the private hosted zone, labeled “resolve [DNS]; endpoint private IP.”

Flow B is drawn with orange solid directed arrows for HTTPS requests and routing on port 443, followed by API invocation. Its numbered path is:
B1: The representative integration caller sends an HTTPS request to Azure Firewall, labeled “HTTPS request [443].”
B2: Azure Firewall routes HTTPS traffic to Azure VPN Gateway, labeled “HTTPS routing [443].”
B3: Azure VPN Gateway routes HTTPS traffic to AWS Site-to-Site VPN across the cloud boundary, labeled “HTTPS routing [443 / IPsec VPN].”
B4: AWS Site-to-Site VPN routes HTTPS traffic to Transit Gateway, labeled “HTTPS routing [443].”
B5: Transit Gateway routes HTTPS traffic to AWS Network Firewall — IDPS, labeled “HTTPS routing [443 / IDPS].”
B6: AWS Network Firewall routes traffic to the execute-api interface VPC endpoint in the egress VPC, labeled “routing [HTTPS 443].”
B7a, B7b, and B7c: The interface VPC endpoint sends HTTPS traffic on port 443 into, respectively, the dev, test, or prod workload account’s private REST API. One environment is selected per request.
B8a, B8b, and B8c: The corresponding dev, test, or prod API Gateway invokes its own environment’s API backend, labeled “invoke [AWS Lambda].”

The interface VPC endpoint is the private entry to the API Gateway APIs. Route 53 performs DNS resolution; no Route 53 outbound endpoint is retained. Route 53 resolver endpoints do not forward HTTPS. DNS queries pass through AWS Network Firewall in this fixture. API access remains subject to each API’s resource policy; the policy rules are not specified.

A firewall allowance table applies to both Azure Firewall AND AWS Network Firewall. Its columns are Environment, Source, Destination, and Port. The rows are: dev, dev spoke subnet, Route 53 inbound endpoint IPs, 53; test, test spoke subnet, Route 53 inbound endpoint IPs, 53; prod, prod spoke subnet, Route 53 inbound endpoint IPs, 53; and dev/test/prod, corresponding spoke subnet, *.execute-api.{region}.amazonaws.com, 443. The architecture parameters {region} and {Route 53 inbound endpoint IPs} are supplied parameters.

The legend states that numbering is independent for each flow and that a/b/c selects dev/test/prod, with one environment per request. A filled arrow means caller to callee or explicitly labeled infrastructure traffic routing. Normal responses are folded into request labels. Boundaries identify architectural domains. No call frequency, detailed authentication mechanism, specific denial/error response, or additional routing behavior is specified.

4.description:
The dynamic deployment diagram describes private cross-cloud API access from Azure to AWS. Azure integration workloads privately call internal AWS API Gateway REST APIs. Flow A resolves DNS; flow B carries the corresponding environment's API request. The architecture has dev, test, and prod environments, and one environment is selected per request.

Azure Cloud is a deployment node containing a DNS extension VNet, a hub VNet, and three separate spoke VNets: dev, test, and prod. Each VNet is a deployment node. The dev spoke is the representative example. It contains a representative integration caller, a container implemented with Azure Function Apps; Logic Apps is an alternative caller. This represents the environment-specific integration workload and selects the corresponding AWS workload account. The dev spoke connects to the hub VNet and to the separate DNS extension VNet. The test and prod spokes each have an integration workload implemented with Function Apps or Logic Apps, use the same representative A/B flow, and connect to the hub VNet and separate DNS extension VNet.

The DNS extension VNet contains a Private Resolver inbound endpoint and a Private Resolver outbound endpoint, both infrastructure nodes of Azure DNS Private Resolver. Its DNS forwarding ruleset is *.execute-api.{region}.amazonaws.com directed to {Route 53 inbound endpoint IPs}. DNS uses port 53, and resolver IPs are parameters. The hub VNet contains Azure Firewall and Azure VPN Gateway, both infrastructure nodes with their corresponding Azure technologies.

AWS Cloud is a deployment node containing a deployment node named Region: {region}. This region contains a network services account and separate dev, test, and prod workload accounts, all deployment nodes.

The network services account contains an Ingress VPC with CIDR 10.1.0.0/20, an Inspection VPC with CIDR 10.2.0.0/24, and an Egress VPC with CIDR 10.3.0.0/20, each a deployment node. The Ingress VPC contains a Route 53 inbound endpoint, an infrastructure node implemented with Amazon Route 53 Resolver, and a private hosted zone, an infrastructure node implemented with Amazon Route 53. The private hosted zone is execute-api.{region}.amazonaws.com and is associated with the ingress VPC. The Inspection VPC contains AWS Network Firewall — IDPS, an infrastructure node implemented with AWS Network Firewall. The Egress VPC contains an execute-api interface VPC endpoint, an infrastructure node implemented with AWS VPC endpoint. This endpoint is the private entry to the API Gateway APIs, with one environment selected per request. The network services account also contains infrastructure nodes AWS Site-to-Site VPN and AWS Transit Gateway, using their corresponding AWS technologies; these are depicted outside the three VPC boundaries.

Transit Gateway attachments are the ingress, inspection, and egress VPCs. Transit Gateway/VPC routing beyond the depicted forwarding path is unspecified. Route 53 performs DNS resolution. No Route 53 outbound endpoint is retained. Resolver endpoints do not forward HTTPS. DNS queries pass through AWS Network Firewall in this fixture.

Each of the dev, test, and prod workload accounts contains its own Internal API software system boundary. Each such boundary contains two containers: an environment-specific private REST API implemented with Amazon API Gateway, and the corresponding environment-specific API backend implemented with AWS Lambda. All three REST APIs are resource policy protected. The Lambda runtimes are unspecified. There are three private REST APIs and three Lambda backends in total. API access remains subject to each API's resource policy; policy rules are not specified.

Flow A is the directed DNS query and DNS routing path, using port 53. The depicted representative caller initiates it from the dev spoke, with the same representative flow applying to the other environments:

1. A1: The representative integration caller queries the Azure Private Resolver inbound endpoint using DNS port 53. The label also includes the reply: private endpoint IP.
2. A2: The Private Resolver inbound endpoint sends an execute-api query to the Private Resolver outbound endpoint using DNS port 53.
3. A3: The Private Resolver outbound endpoint routes DNS on port 53 to Azure Firewall in the hub VNet.
4. A4: Azure Firewall routes DNS on port 53 to Azure VPN Gateway.
5. A5: Azure VPN Gateway routes DNS on port 53 over an IPsec VPN to AWS Site-to-Site VPN, crossing from Azure Cloud into the AWS region's network services account.
6. A6: AWS Site-to-Site VPN routes DNS on port 53 to AWS Transit Gateway.
7. A7: AWS Transit Gateway routes DNS on port 53 through IDPS to AWS Network Firewall in the Inspection VPC.
8. A8: AWS Network Firewall routes DNS on port 53 to the Route 53 inbound endpoint in the Ingress VPC.
9. A9: The Route 53 inbound endpoint sends a resolve operation to the private hosted zone, labeled DNS and endpoint private IP. Together with A1, the diagram identifies the private endpoint IP as the DNS result.

Flow B is the directed HTTPS request/routing path on port 443 followed by API invocation. It starts at the representative Azure integration caller and travels independently of the resolver endpoints:

1. B1: The integration caller makes an HTTPS request on port 443 to Azure Firewall in the hub VNet.
2. B2: Azure Firewall routes HTTPS on port 443 to Azure VPN Gateway.
3. B3: Azure VPN Gateway routes HTTPS on port 443 over an IPsec VPN to AWS Site-to-Site VPN, crossing the cloud boundary into the network services account.
4. B4: AWS Site-to-Site VPN routes HTTPS on port 443 to AWS Transit Gateway.
5. B5: AWS Transit Gateway routes HTTPS on port 443 through IDPS to AWS Network Firewall in the Inspection VPC.
6. B6: AWS Network Firewall performs routing labeled HTTPS 443 to the execute-api interface VPC endpoint in the Egress VPC.
7. B7a, B7b, and B7c are alternative environment-specific HTTPS port 443 calls from that endpoint to the dev, test, and prod private REST APIs respectively. These cross from the network services account into the corresponding workload account and its Internal API boundary. One environment is selected per request.
8. B8a: The dev private REST API invokes the dev API backend using AWS Lambda. B8b: The test private REST API invokes the test API backend using AWS Lambda. B8c: The prod private REST API invokes the prod API backend using AWS Lambda.

The firewall allowance table applies to both Azure Firewall and AWS Network Firewall. Its entries are: dev environment, source dev spoke subnet, destination Route 53 inbound endpoint IPs, port 53; test environment, source test spoke subnet, destination Route 53 inbound endpoint IPs, port 53; prod environment, source prod spoke subnet, destination Route 53 inbound endpoint IPs, port 53; and dev/test/prod, source corresponding spoke subnet, destination *.execute-api.{region}.amazonaws.com, port 443.

The legend distinguishes A as blue dashed DNS queries and DNS traffic routing on port 53, and B as orange solid HTTPS requests/routing on port 443 followed by API invocation. Numbering is independent per flow. Suffixes a/b/c select dev/test/prod, with one environment per request. Filled arrows mean caller to callee or explicitly labeled infrastructure traffic routing. Normal responses are folded into request labels. Boundaries identify architectural domains.

Architecture parameters are {region} and {Route 53 inbound endpoint IPs}. No call frequency, detailed authentication mechanism, specific denial/error response, or additional routing behavior is specified.

judgeNotes.exclusions: Excluded authoring-only instructions (drawing geometry, numbering/color/legend conventions and requested C4 node types), the removed Route 53 outbound endpoint scope, and readout-only statements about absent call frequency/authentication/error details. judgeNotes.findings: L2 explicitly assigns AWS Site-to-Site VPN to the network services account although L0 only assigns Transit Gateway to that account. This added account ownership is critical.
